grounded_facts: Carson Arden appears to Robin Mercer and tells him she loves him, then kisses him.
memories.memory_text: I appeared to Robin Mercer, told him I love him, and kissed him.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer wakes up and tells Darian Wilder that Carson Arden visited him to say she loved him and that his mother was gone.
memories.memory_text: I visited Robin Mercer and told him I loved him and that his mother was gone.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder comforts Robin Mercer after he reports seeing Carson Arden and hearing about his mother's death.
memories.memory_text: I think Robin Mercer was comforted after I told him about his mother, though I wasn't sure how he would take the news.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer enters the house and repeatedly calls out for Carson Arden and his mother, receiving no response.
memories.memory_text: I called out for Carson Arden and Mama when I came back to the house, but no one answered me.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer learns that his mother has died from Mrs. Carter, Owen Calloway who emerges from the bedroom.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mrs. Carter come out from the bedroom and heard her say my mother had died, and I understood it was true.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Carter tells Robin Mercer that his mother has died, delivering the news directly.
memories.memory_text: Mrs. Carter told me that my mother had died when I asked where everyone was.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer stands at his mother Carson Arden's gravesite during the funeral, emotionally bidding her farewell.
A funeral gathering held at an Eastgate Warehouse for Carson Arden, attended mostly by elderly white mourners including her daughter and Robin Mercer.
memories.memory_text: I stood at my mother Carson Arden's gravesite during her funeral, saying my goodbyes as the elderly mourners, including my sister, gathered around.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer speaks aloud about the meaning of losing loved ones, framing loss as a way to understand their importance.
memories.memory_text: I spoke aloud about how we are meant to lose the people we love, because it's how we know how important they are to us.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, hidden in a dresser drawer, experiences a sense of belonging for the first time.
memories.memory_text: I found a home... for the first time, I felt like I belonged somewhere, hidden in that dresser drawer.

grounded_facts: Carson Arden instructs Robin Mercer to stop banging his fork and to use his napkin, enforcing proper dining behavior.
Carson Arden corrects Robin Mercer’s childish use of the fork and reminds him to use a napkin, treating him as both a resident and a child in need of guidance.
memories.memory_text: I remember Carson Arden stopping me from banging my fork, telling me it was for eating, not playing, and reminding me to use my napkin—she treated me like a child who needed to learn how to behave at the table.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, though chronologically a child, is perceived and treated as an Adrian Monroe by the household, participating in dinner among elderly boarders.
memories.memory_text: I noticed how everyone treated me like an Adrian Monroe during dinner, even though I knew I was young—Carson Arden corrected me like the others, and I blended in with the elderly boarders, despite my body being weak and arthritic, with a hearing aid and wisps of white hair.

grounded_facts: An evening dinner at Eastgate Warehouse where boarders, including Robin Mercer, are served by Carson Arden and Sage Hollis.
memories.memory_text: I was at the evening dinner at Eastgate Warehouse, where Carson Arden and Sage Hollis served the boarders, and I remember Carson Arden adjusting my fork and reminding me to use my napkin as if I were one of the elderly residents.

grounded_facts: An elder uses his cane to stop Robin Mercer's wheelchair, expressing disapproval of his movement.
An elder on the porch stops Robin Mercer's wheelchair by inserting his cane into the spokes, halting his movement.
memories.memory_text: I was wheeling my chair back and forth because I wanted to see the street, but one of the elders stopped me by sticking his cane in the spokes of my wheelchair, making it stop suddenly.

grounded_facts: Driven by curiosity, Robin Mercer wheels himself to the edge of the porch to see over the low wall and observes children playing and carriages arriving for a party.
memories.memory_text: I wheeled myself to the edge of the porch because I was curious to see the street—I could see children playing and carriages arriving for a party.

grounded_facts: Carson Arden verbally reprimands Robin Mercer for being at the edge of the porch and pulls him back for safety.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Carson Arden that being at the edge was dangerous when she called out, 'Robin Mercer! That's dangerous... Come back here...!'

grounded_facts: Carson Arden intervenes to pull Robin Mercer back from the edge of the porch, deeming it dangerous, and moves him to a safer location out of sight of the street.
memories.memory_text: I felt my wheelchair being pulled back by Carson Arden, and she moved me away from the edge to a safer spot where I couldn't see the street anymore.

grounded_facts: Carson Arden comforts Robin Mercer by framing individual life paths as different roads toward the same end, affirming his unique journey.
memories.memory_text: I remember Carson Arden telling me that everyone feels different in their own way, and that we're all going the same way but taking different roads—she said I'm on my own road, just like she said, 'You're on your own road, Robin Mercer.'

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer voices his feeling of change and uncertainty about his remaining lifespan, showing emotional dependence on Carson Arden.
memories.memory_text: I told Carson Arden that I feel different from the day before, and I asked her how much longer I have to live because I'm scared and unsure about my future.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis silently enters, signals Robin Mercer, carries him out, and places him in his wheelchair, indicating a routine caregiving transition.
Sage Hollis enters the room silently, signals Robin Mercer, carries him out, and places him in his wheelchair, ending the private moment with Carson Arden.
memories.memory_text: I saw Sage Hollis quietly come into the room, look at me, and I knew it was time—he picked me up and carried me out to my wheelchair, ending my time with Carson Arden.

grounded_facts: An intimate nighttime moment between Robin Mercer and Carson Arden, involving hand-holding and emotional conversation, briefly interrupted by caregiving duties.
memories.memory_text: I held Carson Arden's hand at night, and I told her I loved her very much—she was my mother. Later, Sage Hollis came in and helped me into my wheelchair, taking me out of the room so Carson Arden could rest.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer sits alone in Eastgate Warehouse late at night, listening to the sounds of the sleeping household, feeling safe while observing the quiet routine of the house.
A quiet nighttime moment in Eastgate Warehouse Eastgate Warehouse where Robin Mercer reflects and observes while others sleep.
memories.memory_text: I sat alone in Eastgate Warehouse late at night, listening to the house breathing and the quiet sounds of everyone sleeping—I felt safe in the stillness, just observing the familiar rhythms around me.

grounded_facts: Driven by curiosity, Robin Mercer wheels himself to the window to look outside at the streetlights and the world beyond the gate, seeking to understand what might be dangerous.
memories.memory_text: I wheeled myself over to the window because I was curious about what might be dangerous outside, so I looked at the streetlights and the world beyond the gate to try to understand it.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer's voiceover reports that Valerie Cavendish, a former opera singer, sings Wagnerian opera during the scene.
memories.memory_text: I remember seeing Valerie Cavendish sing Wagnerian opera during the morning ritual; she was a former opera singer and her voice carried beautifully.

grounded_facts: Carson Arden gives Robin Mercer a bath and massages his crippled legs to stimulate movement.
memories.memory_text: I remember Carson Arden giving me a bath and massaging my crippled legs, trying to get me to move them.

grounded_facts: Carson Arden speaks encouragingly to Robin Mercer while massaging his legs, expressing hope that he will walk again.
memories.memory_text: I heard Carson Arden speak encouragingly while she massaged my legs, saying we were going to get me walking again.

grounded_facts: Breakfast is served at six o'clock in Eastgate Warehouse.
memories.memory_text: I remember that breakfast was served promptly at six in Eastgate Warehouse.

grounded_facts: A morning session in Eastgate Warehouse Cedar Grove Motel where Robin Mercer, under Sage Hollis's instruction, learns to cook and read simultaneously.
memories.memory_text: I remember that A morning session in Eastgate Warehouse Cedar Grove Motel where Robin Mercer, under Sage Hollis's instruction, learns to cook and read simultaneously.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis corrects Robin Mercer when he misreads 'v' as 'b' in 'gravy', guiding him to the right pronunciation.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Sage Hollis corrects Robin Mercer when he misreads 'v' as 'b' in 'gravy', guiding him to the right pronunciation.

grounded_facts: Under Sage Hollis's guidance, Robin Mercer practices reading words like 'biscuits' and 'gravy' while also learning cooking measurements, showing progress in both literacy and culinary skills.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Under Sage Hollis's guidance, Robin Mercer practices reading words like 'biscuits' and 'gravy' while also learning cooking measurements, showing progress in both literacy and culinary skills.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer correctly adds four parts butter and two parts flour to determine the total is six, showing understanding of basic math in a practical context.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Robin Mercer correctly adds four parts butter and two parts flour to determine the total is six, showing understanding of basic math in a practical context.

grounded_facts: After Robin Mercer correctly adds four and two, Sage Hollis playfully calls him an 'addin' machine,' acknowledging his correct response.
memories.memory_text: I remember that After Robin Mercer correctly adds four and two, Sage Hollis playfully calls him an 'addin' machine,' acknowledging his correct response.

grounded_facts: An evening moment in the Nolan household where Sage Hollis and Robin Mercer wash and put away dishes, leading to intimate conversation.
memories.memory_text: I remember that evening washing dishes with Sage Hollis, putting away cans and reading labels together, when our conversation turned personal.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis swats Robin Mercer with a dish towel and corrects his misreading of the word 'molasses' on a can label.
memories.memory_text: I misread the word on the can, and I felt the snap of the dish towel as Sage Hollis swatted me and said, "Molasses," correcting my mistake.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis confronts Robin Mercer about underestimating his intelligence and education.
memories.memory_text: I was confronted by Sage Hollis when he asked if I thought he was plain ignorant, making me realize I had underestimated him.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis demonstrates his ability to read and shares that he learned at a young age through his grandfather, who worked for a famous actor.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Sage Hollis that he learned to read at five from his grandfather, who worked for John Wilkes Booth, and he recited lines from a play to show me how deeply he knew them.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis reveals that his grandfather worked for John Wilkes Booth, the assassin of Abraham Lincoln, introducing a dark historical legacy.
memories.memory_text: I remember Sage Hollis telling me that his grandfather worked for John Wilkes Booth, the man who killed Abraham Lincoln.

grounded_facts: The preacher commands Robin Mercer to rise from his wheelchair in the name of God.
memories.memory_text: I heard the preacher, hands on my shoulders, commanding me to rise from my wheelchair in the name of God's glory.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, despite physical difficulty, stands from his wheelchair when commanded by the preacher.
memories.memory_text: I struggled to obey, and with great effort, I stood up from the wheelchair despite my legs being weak and unsteady.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer takes a few steps but collapses due to arthritic legs giving out.
memories.memory_text: I took a couple of shaky steps, but my arthritic legs gave out and I fell to the floor.

grounded_facts: The preacher forbids the aides from helping Robin Mercer after his fall.
memories.memory_text: I heard the preacher shout 'Don't touch him!' after I fell, so I knew no one was allowed to help me.

grounded_facts: After lying on the floor, Robin Mercer slowly rises again under the preacher's command.
memories.memory_text: I was lying on the floor, and though my legs ached and trembled, I heard the preacher's command and slowly pushed myself up to my feet.

grounded_facts: Carson Arden joins Robin Mercer and urges him forward during his walk.
memories.memory_text: I felt Carson Arden come beside me and heard her say, 'Let the Lord carry you,' urging me forward as I struggled to keep moving.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer hobbles across the stage with support from Carson Arden and the preacher, completing the ritual walk.
memories.memory_text: With Carson Arden and the preacher beside me, I hobbled across the stage, step by step, and made it to the end, met by a roar of amens from the congregation.

grounded_facts: The preacher collapses and dies from a spontaneous coronary after exalting God.
memories.memory_text: I saw the preacher exalting God, and then he suddenly collapsed right in front of me, falling flat on his face and lying there completely still—I realized he had died from a heart attack.

grounded_facts: A gospel healing service in a Eastgate Warehouse church tent where individuals seek divine intervention for physical and spiritual ailments.
memories.memory_text: I remember being wheeled into the church tent in Eastgate Warehouse, surrounded by people seeking healing, with the preacher exalting in God's name and the nurses in crisp uniforms ready to assist.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer and the elderly residents sit on the porch at dusk, silently observing the end of the day, reflecting a state of pure being.
A quiet gathering of Robin Mercer and the elderly residents on the front porch at dusk, watching the sunset and enjoying simple companionship.
memories.memory_text: I sat on the porch with the others at dusk, watching the sun go down in silence, feeling the peace in our simple companionship and stillness.

grounded_facts: One of the elderly individuals farts, underscoring the simplicity and unfiltered nature of life on the porch.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting on the porch with the others, enjoying the quiet, when one of the elderly men let out a fart, breaking the silence in a way that somehow felt honest and real.

grounded_facts: Sage Hollis explains to Robin Mercer who Evan Arden is and that he will be staying at the house temporarily.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Sage Hollis that Evan Arden is an acquaintance of an acquaintance of hers and that he'll be staying with us in the staff quarters for a while.

grounded_facts: Mr. Evan Arden begins staying at Eastgate Warehouse in the staff quarters, introduced through Sage Hollis's explanation to Robin Mercer.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mr. Evan Arden begins staying at Eastgate Warehouse in the staff quarters, introduced through Sage Hollis's explanation to Robin Mercer.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden recounts his past hardships, including being captured by cannibals and losing two wives, which elicits reactions ranging from fear to laughter.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Evan Arden recounts his past hardships, including being captured by cannibals and losing two wives, which elicits reactions ranging from fear to laughter.

grounded_facts: After noticing Robin Mercer watching him through the window, Evan Arden immediately moves out of sight.
Upon noticing Robin Mercer watching through the window, Evan Arden quickly moves out of sight.
memories.memory_text: I saw Evan Arden notice me watching him through the window, and he quickly turned away and moved out of sight.

grounded_facts: A group of old people gather on the lawn to listen to Evan Arden tell stories about his past experiences, including captivity and loss.
memories.memory_text: I remember that A group of old people gather on the lawn to listen to Evan Arden tell stories about his past experiences, including captivity and loss.

grounded_facts: A clandestine, informal gathering under the stairs where Evan Arden shares a critical, satirical account of his experience at the 1904 World's Fair with members of the household staff.
Robin Mercer silently watches Evan Arden's storytelling from a distance, becoming an unintended audience to a private, subversive narrative.

Evan Arden delivers a satirical and critical narrative about white people and the absurdity of their treatment of him and others at the 1904 World's Fair, bonding with the staff through shared irony and resistance.
memories.memory_text: I was lying by the stairs with my army men when I heard Evan Arden's voice, so I got my canes and went to look; I stayed quiet as I watched him under the stairs telling the staff stories about the 1904 World's Fair, mocking the white people who put him on display, and I saw them all laugh together at how absurd it was.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer overhears Evan Arden telling a subversive version of his past experience at the 1904 World's Fair, mocking white people and revealing the dehumanizing conditions of the exhibition, which contrasts with any prior public persona.
memories.memory_text: I overheard Evan Arden telling a version of his past that mocked white authority and revealed how dehumanizing the World's Fair was, and when he turned and noticed me, I knew I had to retreat quickly on my canes before he could say anything.

grounded_facts: After Evan Arden senses his presence, Robin Mercer quickly withdraws on his canes, indicating fear or desire to avoid confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I quickly retreated on my canes when I realized Evan Arden sensed my presence, not wanting to be seen or confronted.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden offers Robin Mercer a chance to go out for a cold root beer, creating a moment of decision.
memories.memory_text: Evan Arden asked me if I wanted to get a cold root beer, offering me a chance to go out.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer echoes that going out is dangerous, indicating internal conflict.
memories.memory_text: I said it's dangerous, because I truly felt the risk in going outside.

grounded_facts: Despite initial hesitation and a warning that it's dangerous, Robin Mercer chooses to follow Evan Arden outside the house.
memories.memory_text: Even though I was afraid, I took up my canes and followed Evan Arden outside.

grounded_facts: An impromptu invitation by Evan Arden for Robin Mercer to go out for a cold root beer, leading to Robin Mercer leaving the house.
memories.memory_text: I was told we were going out for a cold root beer, and that’s why I ended up leaving the house.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden tells Robin Mercer to hurry as they exit the house and approach the street.
memories.memory_text: I remember Evan Arden telling me to hurry as we left the house and headed toward the street.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden causes a streetcar to stop suddenly by running in front of it and waving his arms.
memories.memory_text: I saw Evan Arden suddenly run into the street and wave his arms in front of a moving streetcar, making it stop abruptly so we could board.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer and Evan Arden are riding together on a streetcar in Eastgate Warehouse, seated behind a 'Coloreds' barrier.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting with Evan Arden on the streetcar in Eastgate Warehouse, behind the 'Coloreds' barrier, feeling the weight of where we were allowed to sit.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden shows Robin Mercer a newspaper clipping and describes his degrading experience of being exhibited in a cage with monkeys, including how he was forced to scare children.
memories.memory_text: Evan Arden showed me a newspaper clipping and told me how he was forced to live in a cage with monkeys, filing his teeth like a cannibal and scaring children as part of the act.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden reenacts how he was made to scare children in his cage by baring his filed teeth and charging at nearby schoolchildren.
memories.memory_text: I saw Evan Arden suddenly jump up and bare his filed teeth, charging at nearby schoolchildren just like he was made to do in the zoo, and I watched them scream in fear.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer chokes on Coca-Cola, and Evan Arden provides a handkerchief to help him recover.
memories.memory_text: I took too big a sip of Coca-Cola and ended up choking, coke pouring out of my nose, and Evan Arden helped me by giving me his handkerchief to clean up.

grounded_facts: A reflective dialogue between Evan Arden and Robin Mercer on the nature of loneliness, identity, and human connection, taking place on a park bench.
memories.memory_text: Evan Arden told me that everyone is alone in their own way, no matter how they look, and that there's nothing wrong with being alone—he said even fat, skinny, tall, or white people are just as alone as we are, but they're scared to admit it.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden imparts a personal realization to Robin Mercer about the universal experience of loneliness and the courage to accept being alone.
Evan Arden tells Robin Mercer that everyone is fundamentally alone, regardless of appearance, and that there is nothing wrong with being alone.
memories.memory_text: I remember Evan Arden telling me that everyone is alone, no matter how they look, and that there’s nothing wrong with being alone — he said even fat, skinny, tall, and white people are just as alone as us, but they’re scared to admit it.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden reflects on his childhood river, expressing a desire to return and sit beside it again.
memories.memory_text: I remember Evan Arden telling me how he thought about the river he grew up on and said it would be good to sit by it again.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden checks his watch and abruptly stands up, indicating a decision to depart from the park bench where he was sitting with Robin Mercer.
memories.memory_text: I saw Evan Arden check his watch and suddenly get up, which made me realize he had decided to leave the park bench where we were sitting.

grounded_facts: Filamena expresses affection and familiarity upon seeing Evan Arden.
memories.memory_text: I saw Filamena show clear affection for Evan Arden when she called him 'my little man' and asked if he was ready, speaking to him sweetly.

grounded_facts: A chance encounter on a street corner in Eastgate Warehouse where Evan Arden reunites with Darian Calloway named Filamena while accompanied by Robin Mercer.
memories.memory_text: I was with Evan Arden when we came to a street corner in Eastgate Warehouse and he met a tall octoroon woman named Filamena, who smiled broadly at him and greeted him warmly.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden introduces Robin Mercer to Filamena, briefly establishing their presence together.
memories.memory_text: I remember Evan Arden introducing me to Filamena by saying, 'Filamena, Mr. Robin Mercer,' and in that moment, I realized I was being formally presented as part of their brief encounter.

grounded_facts: Evan Arden asks Robin Mercer if he can find his own way home, effectively ending their time together and leaving Robin Mercer alone.
memories.memory_text: Evan Arden asked me if I could find my own way home, and I didn't say anything—he just left after that.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer is abandoned at the corner by Evan Arden, who departs with Filamena, leaving Robin Mercer to find his own way home.
memories.memory_text: I was left standing on the street corner when Evan Arden walked off with Filamena, his arm around her waist, both of them laughing as I looked around trying to get my bearings.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, though uncertain, starts walking alone along Bourbon Street using his canes, showing determination.

memories.memory_text: I remember we were the first to arrive at the scene after a transport carrying 900 men was hit by a torpedo, and as our the blue box reached the site, I saw the vessel sinking quickly with a gaping hole in its side and fuel oil burning on the water.

grounded_facts: The crew visually confronts the horrifying aftermath of the torpedo attack, seeing numerous dead bodies and the final moments of the sinking vessel.
memories.memory_text: I saw the bodies of dead men floating in the water, more and more of them, until we were moving through a carpet of bodies, and I witnessed the final moments as the transport slipped silently into the sea, men trapped in the burning black oil.

grounded_facts: Robin Monroe, fatally wounded, dies after a final conversation with Robin Mercer.
memories.memory_text: I saw him lying there, covered in blood and trembling, and I stayed with him, holding his hand until he passed, his eyes finding some kind of peace at the end.

memories.memory_text: I felt a deep sense of mourning for my comrades after the 'Chelsea' sank, and when I saw the hummingbird near the wreath, it reminded me how far we were from life and home.

memories.memory_text: I arrived at Eastgate Warehouse with my suitcase, feeling the weight of my journey behind me, and noticed the old blind dog recognizing me as I came up the walk, now returning as a man in his fifties who barely resembled the one who left.

memories.memory_text: I asked the young girl if her mother was home, and she told me she was getting supper ready, so I knew she was inside and likely to be there for a while.

memories.memory_text: I felt Carson Arden touch the bullet scar on my forehead and say, 'You seen some pain,' and in that moment, I knew she recognized what I'd been through.

memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder taking my hand and suggesting we go back to the house or get a room somewhere, trying to lead me toward the dark of the park.

memories.memory_text: I told Darian Wilder to go back to New York and be with the people she's fond of, because I believe you can only be young once.

memories.memory_text: I saw how Darian Wilder reached out to me, asking to go back to the house or get a room, and when I turned her down, she asked if I thought I was too old for her — I could tell it hurt her.

memories.memory_text: I realized I didn't need glasses anymore, my vision had sharpened on its own.

memories.memory_text: I stood naked in front of the mirror and saw my hair growing in with little gray, and I noticed my sense of smell was sharper, my hearing more acute, and that I could walk further and faster than before.

memories.memory_text: I heard someone knock and call my name, so I opened the door and saw my father; he asked if I remembered him, and then said, 'Welcome home, my friend,' which struck me deeply as he stood there, frail and uncertain.

memories.memory_text: I remember sitting with Adrian Thorne at a crowded Eastgate Warehouse steakhouse, the bar filled with men bearing war wounds, as we shared thick steaks and drinks and talked about personal matters.

memories.memory_text: I heard Adrian Thorne tell me how the war had been good to his the wooden box business, saying they went from making forty thousand buttons a day to two hundred fifty thousand, employed ten times as many workers, and were operating around the clock.

memories.memory_text: I remember Adrian Thorne telling me how he was frightened about dying alone and didn't have any people, and he asked if I would keep him company when possible.

memories.memory_text: I told Adrian Thorne I was sorry to hear about his illness and that I'd do what I could to be there for him.

memories.memory_text: I asked Adrian Thorne what he meant by 'our family,' because I needed to know where I truly belonged.

memories.memory_text: Adrian Thorne told me he was my father and that I was born the night the Great War ended, and that my mother died giving birth to me—he said he left me because he thought I was a monster and was too afraid to keep me.

grounded_facts: After learning his mother died in childbirth, Robin Mercer quietly asks, 'My mother?', expressing shock and emerging grief.
memories.memory_text: When I heard my mother had died in childbirth, I could barely speak—so I just whispered, 'My mother?' as if saying it might make it real.

grounded_facts: Adrian Thorne gives Robin Mercer a tour of the the wooden box factory at night, using the setting to deliver a personal and emotional confession about their familial relationship.
memories.memory_text: I walked through the quiet factory with Adrian Thorne at night, and the whole time I could feel something heavy coming, like the machines were holding their breath along with me.

memories.memory_text: I was told by Adrian Thorne that my mother's name was Finley Hayes, that she was twenty, from Dublin, and worked in my grandfather's Cedar Grove Motel, and that her father was a chimney sweep who died in the 1900 flu epidemic, and that she came to Eastgate Warehouse with her family in 1903.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer confronts Adrian Thorne about not being told the truth earlier, expressing hurt and betrayal.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Adrian Thorne, asking him why he never told me the truth—I felt hurt and betrayed by his silence.

memories.memory_text: Adrian Thorne told me I could come back to the family, saying we could make up for lost time and that he planned to leave everything to me, trying to win me over with promises of belonging and inheritance.

memories.memory_text: I walked with Adrian Thorne through the hallway filled with family photographs, and I saw him point out relatives while sharing stories about his past, including how much he loved my mother and the day he married her, but when he asked me to stay and offered me everything, I turned my back and left.

memories.memory_text: I told Adrian Thorne I better go, and when he asked where, I said home—then I turned and walked out, knowing I was leaving behind his offer and any chance of a real father-son bond.

memories.memory_text: I remember Carson Arden telling me, in a fit of anger, that my father didn't deserve forgiveness and mocked his attempt to come back into my life, saying she'd never forgive him and that only God could.

memories.memory_text: I remember Lane Dalton telling me he was struck by lightning seven times and said it was God’s way of reminding him to appreciate life.

memories.memory_text: After Lane Dalton left, I went over to the window and looked out, just like I used to do as a boy.

memories.memory_text: I carried my father down to the dock and helped him sit in the deck chair, and we both watched the sunrise together; I was there when he quietly shut his eyes for the last time.

memories.memory_text: I stood at Carson Arden's gravesite in that Eastgate Warehouse, surrounded by elderly mourners, and saw her daughter there, now in her early thirties, paying her respects.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer stands at his mother Carson Arden's gravesite during the funeral, emotionally bidding her farewell.
memories.memory_text: I stood over my mother Carson Arden's grave and said my goodbyes, feeling the weight of her absence as I honored her one last time.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer speaks aloud about the meaning of losing loved ones, framing loss as a way to understand their importance.
memories.memory_text: I spoke aloud, saying that we are meant to lose the people we love—it's how we know how important they are to us.

memories.memory_text: I sold my father's house on Blaine Street so we could have memories of our own.

grounded_facts: A formal viewing of Eastgate Warehouse by potential buyers, accompanied by Robin Mercer and a real estate agent, marking a transition in ownership.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the formal viewing of Eastgate Warehouse as the pregnant woman and her older husband were shown around by the real estate agent, marking the beginning of the house's transition to new ownership.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer shows a pregnant woman and her older husband around Eastgate Warehouse, initiating a viewing process that highlights emotional and historical weight.
memories.memory_text: I was directly involved in showing the pregnant woman and her older husband around Eastgate Warehouse, guiding them through the viewing process and highlighting its history and emotional weight.

grounded_facts: Linden Carver assumes Robin Mercer has fond memories and finds it hard to let go of the house, expressing sympathy.
memories.memory_text: I was told it must be hard for me to give up the house, that I must have a lot of fond memories there.

grounded_facts: The older man arrives late, sees his wife, and hugs and kisses her tenderly, highlighting their intimate bond despite visible age difference.
memories.memory_text: I saw the older man arrive late and hug his wife, kissing her tenderly, and I was acutely aware of how great their age difference was.

grounded_facts: The pregnant woman expresses strong emotional attachment to the house, indicating intent to purchase and settle there with her husband.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the pregnant woman express her deep emotional attachment to the house, saying they would be happy there, clearly indicating her intent to purchase and make it their home.

grounded_facts: Linden Carver admires the family photographs, noting the long family history associated with the house.
memories.memory_text: I saw Linden Carver pause in the hallway, clearly taken with the family photographs, and she said, 'Oh, what a long family history you have...'

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer responds to Linden Carver's admiration of the family photos by saying they 'come with the house,' indicating emotional detachment.
memories.memory_text: I told her the photos 'come with the house,' because that's all they really are—part of the property, not something personal I hold onto.

memories.memory_text: I remember that An informal picnic arranged by Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder inside the living room of the townhouse.

memories.memory_text: I remember that Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder have a picnic on the virtually empty living room floor.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder jointly commit to never sleeping or waking at the same time, reinforcing their unique bond.
Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder vow never to go to bed or wake up at the same time, establishing a ritual of asynchronous rest.
memories.memory_text: I remember making a vow with Darian Wilder that we'd never go to bed or wake up at the same time, a promise that became our way of being close yet independent.

grounded_facts: An ongoing intimate cohabitation of Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder living together on a mattress on the floor, engaging in daily and intimate activities.
memories.memory_text: I recall how Darian Wilder and I lived together on a mattress on the floor, sharing everything—sleeping, talking, eating, reading, making love—our whole world contained in that simple space.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder becomes emotionally overwhelmed while observing a young swimmer, confronting her own physical decline and mortality, leading to tears.
memories.memory_text: I saw Darian Wilder start to cry while she was watching a young girl swim laps, completely in tune with her body, and I realized she was confronting her own physical decline and the passing years.

grounded_facts: A meeting between Darian Wilder and Robin Mercer at a public swimming pool during the day, where Darian Wilder swims and observes a young girl, leading to an emotional conversation about aging.
memories.memory_text: I came to meet Darian Wilder at the pool that day, and I saw her resting by the edge after swimming, clearly moved by something.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer notices Darian Wilder is crying and points it out, initiating emotional engagement.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Darian Wilder was crying and said, 'You're crying...' to point it out.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder responds to Robin Mercer's observation by attributing her tears to chlorine, masking her deeper emotional distress.
memories.memory_text: I was told it was just the chlorine, so I learned she was masking her real feelings.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer offers Darian Wilder consolation by reframing her past dance career as a rare and meaningful choice constrained by time, independent of her accident.
Robin Mercer tells Darian Wilder that her dance career was a rare and valuable choice, and that she would have eventually faced the same emotional place regardless of her accident.
memories.memory_text: I offered Darian Wilder consolation by telling her she chose something so special and unique with her dance career, and that there was only a short time she could have done it — that even if nothing had happened, she would eventually be in the same place emotionally.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder directly states her discomfort with growing old, revealing her vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: I heard Darian Wilder say, 'I don't like getting old,' and I could feel her vulnerability in that moment.

grounded_facts: A quiet, intimate moment between Darian Wilder and Robin Mercer in a dance studio at night, marked by reflection, dance, and emotional revelation.
memories.memory_text: I was in the dance studio at night, quietly watching Darian Wilder as she danced alone, and I felt the stillness between us fill with something deep and unspoken.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer affirms Darian Wilder's beauty as a dancer, reinforcing emotional intimacy.
memories.memory_text: I told Darian Wilder, 'You're still beautiful to watch,' and meant every word—her grace moved me in a way I couldn't explain.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder notes that she and Robin Mercer are nearly the same age and will meet in the middle in three years, highlighting their opposing life trajectories.
memories.memory_text: Darian Wilder told me that we're almost the same age and that in three years we'll meet in the middle, and I realized how our lives are moving in opposite directions.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer asks Darian Wilder to remain in her current pose so he can remember their moment together.
memories.memory_text: I asked her to stay just like that because I wanted to remember how we looked together right then, knowing moments like this don't last.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder discloses to Robin Mercer that she is pregnant, a significant emotional and narrative turning point given their age trajectories.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder telling me she was pregnant, saying she thought she was too old, but it was true.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer reacts to the pregnancy news by embracing Darian Wilder with gratitude and emotion.
memories.memory_text: I held her close, touching her face, overwhelmed with gratitude and emotion when I heard the news.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder tells Robin Mercer she overheard Avery Sinclair use a male pronoun, indicating a subtle shift in her awareness.
Darian Wilder mentions that she overheard Avery Sinclair accidentally using a male pronoun, hinting at a revelation about Robin Mercer's true identity or condition.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder telling me she thought she heard Avery Sinclair slip and say 'he,' which made me realize she might be starting to suspect something about me.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer watches a father sitting with his child on the streetcar, triggering an emotional or reflective response.
memories.memory_text: I saw a father sitting with his child on the streetcar, and something about that moment caught my attention and stirred a deep feeling inside me.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder prompts Robin Mercer to open up about his deepest fear, initiating a vulnerable conversation.
memories.memory_text: I recall Darian Wilder looking at me and asking, 'What's your worst fear?'—that’s what made me start to share what I’d been holding inside.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer reveals his deep fear that if their child inherits his condition, he would be more like a little brother than a father, expressing concerns about role reversal and dependency.
memories.memory_text: I told Darian Wilder I was afraid—if our child inherited my condition, I wouldn’t be their father, I’d be more like a little brother, and I couldn’t bear the thought of my own child picking me up from school or babysitting me.

grounded_facts: An intimate late-night conversation between Darian Wilder and Robin Mercer in a Eastgate Warehouse diner, where they discuss fears, love, and the possibility of having a child together.
memories.memory_text: I remember that quiet night in the diner with Darian Wilder, just the two of us talking over coffee and her sundae, when she asked me what my worst fear was and I finally opened up.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder declares her determination to make their relationship and potential parenthood work, accepting all consequences of Robin Mercer's condition.
Darian Wilder comforts Robin Mercer by affirming that he will be a father for as long as he can, and that loving him is worth all consequences.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder telling me she was going to make our relationship work, no matter what, and that she wanted to have a child with me. She said I would be a father for as long as I could, and that loving me was worth all the consequences.

grounded_facts: After seeing Shawn Dalton's achievement on TV, Robin Mercer internally shifts toward hope and acceptance, symbolizing his readiness to believe that 'anything is possible'.
memories.memory_text: I saw Shawn Dalton swimming on the news, and it made me smile—sitting there, I started to believe that maybe anything is possible.

grounded_facts: After internal reflection, Robin Mercer responds affirmatively when Darian Wilder asks if he's ready to leave, symbolizing his emotional readiness to proceed with their journey.
memories.memory_text: When Darian Wilder asked if I was ready, I said yes—I knew in that moment I was finally ready to move forward with her.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder calls out to Robin Mercer after falling, signaling distress and need for help.
memories.memory_text: I heard Darian Wilder call out to me, her voice faint but urgent, needing help right away.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder falls while on the stairs, resulting in blood on her nightdress and a spilled glass of milk.
memories.memory_text: I ran to her and saw Darian Wilder sitting on the stairs, blood on her nightdress and milk spilled on the carpet.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder indicates that labor has started as a result of the fall or independently.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Darian Wilder that Rowan Hayes was coming, as she called out to me after her fall.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer calls for emergency medical help after discovering Darian Wilder injured on the stairs.
memories.memory_text: I was getting dressed when I heard Darian Wilder call out, so I ran to find her sitting on the stairs after a fall; I immediately grabbed the phone and called for an ambulance, telling them my wife was seven months pregnant and hurt, then rushed back to hold her hand.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer hurries to Darian Wilder's side and takes her hand as she is injured and in labor.
memories.memory_text: I hurried to Darian Wilder's side and took her hand when I saw her fallen on the stairs, injured and in labor.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder gives birth to a Jamie Rivers girl weighing five pounds four ounces.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Darian Wilder gave birth to our Jamie Rivers girl, who weighed five pounds four ounces.

grounded_facts: The doctor confirms to Robin Mercer that Rowan Hayes is healthy, alleviating his concern.
memories.memory_text: I was told by the doctor that Rowan Hayes is healthy in every way, and I felt relieved hearing her say that.

grounded_facts: A doctor visits Darian Wilder and Robin Mercer at home after the birth of their child to check on Rowan Hayes's health and provide postnatal care.
memories.memory_text: I was there with Darian Wilder when the young woman doctor came to check on Rowan Hayes after she was born, and I asked if everything was alright.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer kisses Rowan Hayes's head, expressing love and connection.
memories.memory_text: I kissed Rowan Hayes's head as I looked at her, feeling a deep love and connection to my child.

grounded_facts: Finley Hayes (in voiceover) reveals that Rowan Hayes was named after her mother.
memories.memory_text: I heard Finley Hayes’s voice-over saying they named Rowan Hayes after her mother, so I learned Rowan Hayes’s name is Finley Hayes.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder has given birth to a healthy Jamie Rivers girl named Finley Hayes, who is now nursing.
memories.memory_text: I stood beside Darian Wilder and saw our Rowan Hayes on her chest; the doctor confirmed she was healthy, I kissed her head, and I held Darian Wilder's hand as she began nursing our daughter Finley Hayes.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer looks at his reflection and notices he appears young (34 years old) despite being in his 51st year, while observing Darian Wilder showing signs of aging.
memories.memory_text: I looked at my reflection and saw that I still appear young, only about 34, even though I'm in my 51st year, and then I looked at Darian Wilder and noticed the signs of aging on her.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder awakens and senses that Robin Mercer is deeply troubled, then watches him sleep, becoming troubled herself for different reasons.
memories.memory_text: I could feel Darian Wilder wake up and sense that I was deeply troubled, and later I realized she had watched me sleep, becoming troubled herself, though I was trying to hide how I felt.

grounded_facts: A casual daytime gathering in a Eastgate Warehouse park where Robin Mercer, Darian Wilder, and Finley Hayes spend time together.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting in the park with Finley Hayes while she played in the sandbox, and I had to stop her from eating sand; then Darian Wilder came over and joined us.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer expresses the idea that Finley Hayes needs a real father to grow up with, indicating his intention to distance himself from the role.
memories.memory_text: I told Darian Wilder that I think she should find a real father for Finley Hayes because she needs someone to grow old with, and she needs a father, not a playmate.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder interprets Robin Mercer's suggestion about a father as an intention to leave her and directly confronts him.
memories.memory_text: I said Darian Wilder didn't need another child to raise, and I realized she interpreted that as me planning to leave her.

grounded_facts: When confronted by Darian Wilder about leaving, Robin Mercer does not respond, confirming her fears through inaction.
memories.memory_text: I stayed silent when Darian Wilder confronted me about leaving, confirming her fears without speaking.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder pleads with Robin Mercer not to leave, but he remains silent, effectively rejecting her emotional needs.
memories.memory_text: Darian Wilder pleaded with me not to leave, asking me twice, but I remained silent, rejecting her emotional needs.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer sits with Rowan Hayes on his chest in the backyard, indicating a moment of connection between father and child.
memories.memory_text: I remember sitting in the backyard with Rowan Hayes on my chest, feeling her little breaths against me as we shared that quiet moment together.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder stops cleaning and watches Robin Mercer with Rowan Hayes through the window, suggesting emotional or reflective engagement.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Darian Wilder watching us through the window while she was cleaning, and I could tell she was really seeing us—me with our Jamie Rivers.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder cleaning up after the party while the house is empty and guests have left.
memories.memory_text: I figured Darian Wilder was cleaning up after the party once everyone had left, since the house was quiet and she was alone inside.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer whispers to his sleeping daughter that he loves her before leaving.
memories.memory_text: I whispered to my sleeping daughter that I love her, wanting her to know even if she wouldn't remember.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer departs from the bedroom and the family home, finalizing his decision to leave Darian Wilder and their daughter.
memories.memory_text: I departed from the bedroom and the family home, finalizing my decision to leave Darian Wilder and our daughter behind.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder stirs and looks at Robin Mercer with a look of acceptance as he is about to leave.
memories.memory_text: As I was about to leave the bedroom, I saw Darian Wilder stir and look at me with a quiet acceptance, knowing she understood this was my path.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer sells assets and deposits the proceeds into an account for Darian Wilder, leaving a bank the black radio and house key as evidence.
memories.memory_text: I sold the summer house on Lake Pontchartrain, my share of Lakeside Academy, and the sailboat, putting all the proceeds into an account for Darian Wilder, and I left the bank the black radio and house key on the dresser so she'd know.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer leaves his home on a motorcycle with minimal belongings, marking a departure from his current life situation.
memories.memory_text: I took the old motorcycle out of the garage, started it up, and rode away with just the clothes on my back, leaving everything else behind.

grounded_facts: Through a recorded voiceover, Robin Mercer offers Finley Hayes a message of hope, freedom, and self-determination, framed as a wish for her future.
memories.memory_text: I was told that my recorded message would reach Finley Hayes, so I made sure to express hope and freedom, wishing her the courage to live the life she wants and start over if she needs to.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer's voiceover plays, delivering a philosophical and hopeful message about life, change, and self-determination, accompanied by a montage of his travels around the world.
memories.memory_text: I shared my thoughts on life, change, and self-determination in a recorded message, reflecting on my travels around the world.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder realizes the young man who entered the dance studio is Robin Mercer, leading to an emotional confrontation after many years.
memories.memory_text: I saw the young man at the door and realized it was Robin Mercer, and I couldn't believe how young he looked — I asked him why he came back after all these years.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder confronts Robin Mercer emotionally, asking for his reason for returning after so many years.
memories.memory_text: I saw Darian Wilder again after all these years, and she was shocked—I could tell she barely recognized me. She asked me why I came back, her voice trembling, and I could feel the weight of everything left unsaid between us.

grounded_facts: The end-of-night cleanup at the dance studio in Eastgate Warehouse, where parents pick up children and Darian Wilder closes up the space.
memories.memory_text: I was cleaning up the dance studio after class, picking up jackets with my toes, when the door opened and Finley Hayes came rushing in.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer reaches out and takes Finley Hayes's hand upon meeting her, expressing a need to connect physically.
memories.memory_text: When I met Finley Hayes, I reached out and took her hand because I needed to feel that connection—she’s my daughter, and in that moment, touching her made it real.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder presents Robin Mercer to her husband Tristan Mercer, identifying him as a family friend.
memories.memory_text: I was introduced by Darian Wilder to her husband Tristan Mercer as a friend of the family.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder admits to Robin Mercer that he was right about needing a father for their daughter, accepting her own limitations in raising both him and Finley Hayes.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder telling me that I was right to leave because our daughter needed a father, and she admitted she couldn't have raised both of us.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer discloses that he is staying at the Pontchartrain Hotel and has no plan for what to do next.
memories.memory_text: I told Darian Wilder I was staying at the Pontchartrain Hotel on the avenue and that I had no idea what I was going to do next.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer opens the door to find Darian Wilder standing there, which startles him.
memories.memory_text: I opened the door and was startled to see Darian Wilder standing there.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder seeks permission to come into Robin Mercer's hotel room.
memories.memory_text: I heard her ask, 'May I come in?' and I remember her voice right then.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer gently stops Darian Wilder from saying 'Nothing lasts' by putting a finger to her lips and shaking his head.
memories.memory_text: I gently put a finger to Darian Wilder's lips and shook my head to stop her from saying 'Nothing lasts,' knowing that some things do.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer tells Darian Wilder he never stopped loving her, affirming emotional continuity.
memories.memory_text: I told Darian Wilder, 'I never once stopped loving you,' to make sure she knew my love for her has always been constant.

grounded_facts: A private, emotionally intense meeting between Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder in a hotel room at night, marked by vulnerability and reconnection.
memories.memory_text: I was with Darian Wilder in my room that night, and I remember helping her off with her coat, kissing her, and undressing together—we stood there naked, just the two of us, and I felt something deep and quiet between us.

grounded_facts: After emotional exchange, Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder undress and stand naked together, leading to implied sexual intimacy.
memories.memory_text: I was startled when I opened the door and saw Darian Wilder, but I helped her off with her coat, kissed her, and we undressed each other, standing there naked together—me, the older man, and her, so young—and I kissed her again, feeling the quiet truth of being fully exposed, both physically and emotionally.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer recalls the feel, taste, smell, and touch of Darian Wilder as part of his affirmation of love.
memories.memory_text: I remembered the feel, the taste, the way I breathed her in when I kissed her—sensations I know I'll never forget because of how deeply I love her.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder exchange a final wave as she departs in a taxi, both sensing it is their last farewell.
Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder silently wave to each other as she leaves in a taxi, acknowledging their final parting.
memories.memory_text: I stood at the window watching Darian Wilder get into the taxi, and when she turned to wave, I waved back — we didn’t say a word, but I knew it was our final goodbye.

grounded_facts: The social worker acknowledges Darian Wilder's presence and introduces himself formally.
memories.memory_text: I remember the social worker introducing himself to me, saying his name was Owen Colter Hernandez from the Orleans Parish department of Child Welfare Services.

grounded_facts: A social worker gives Valerie Bellamy a journal belonging to Robin Mercer, found with him when discovered in a condemned building.
memories.memory_text: I was told that the red watch had been found with Robin Mercer when he was discovered in a condemned building, and the social worker gave it to me.

grounded_facts: The social worker informs Valerie Bellamy that Robin Mercer was found in poor health, disoriented, and possibly autistic.
memories.memory_text: I learned that Robin Mercer was in very poor health, didn't seem to know who or where he was, and that the doctors thought he might be autistic.

grounded_facts: Valerie Bellamy agrees to let Robin Mercer stay at the house, acknowledging him as family.
Valerie Bellamy emphasizes Robin Mercer's family connection to justify offering him shelter.
memories.memory_text: I told Mr. Hernandez that Robin Mercer was family, and I offered him a place to stay because he is blood, and that’s what matters.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer asks Darian Wilder if she knows the song he is trying to play, indicating a desire for connection or validation.
memories.memory_text: I asked Darian Wilder if she knew the song I was trying to play, hoping she might connect with it.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder touches Robin Mercer's back in a gesture of affection or comfort, but he shrinks away from her touch.
memories.memory_text: When Darian Wilder touched my back, I pulled away—I didn’t want her hand there, even if she meant it kindly.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder tells Robin Mercer her name in an attempt to trigger recognition or establish identity.
memories.memory_text: Darian Wilder told me her name, as if it were supposed to mean something to me, but I didn’t recognize her.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, appearing as a 12-year-old, does not recognize Darian Wilder upon her entrance and initial interaction.
memories.memory_text: I wasn’t sure who Darian Wilder was when she came in, and even after she said her name, she didn’t ring a bell.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder sits beside Robin Mercer on the piano bench as he attempts to play; a quiet moment of attempted reconnection unfolds.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder sitting beside me on the piano bench, saying she’d like to hear me play.

grounded_facts: After sitting together, Robin Mercer remarks that something about Darian Wilder's eyes feels familiar from long ago.
memories.memory_text: I remember telling Darian Wilder that there was something about her eyes that felt familiar from a long time ago.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, at eight years old but mentally regressing, becomes confused about having eaten breakfast and lashes out in anger, throwing things and accusing others of lying.
memories.memory_text: I was so confused about whether I had eaten breakfast—I felt like a child again, losing control—and when someone said I already ate, I got angry and threw things, yelling that they were all liars.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, disoriented and frustrated, verbally accuses the people around him of lying about his breakfast.
memories.memory_text: I accused the people around me of lying when they said I'd already eaten breakfast, because I didn't remember it and felt they were deceiving me.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder acknowledges Robin Mercer's helplessness with compassion and offers comfort.
memories.memory_text: I told her, 'I can't help it. I can't help this,' and she responded with compassion, saying, 'I know you can't,' which made me feel understood in that moment.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder enters Cedar Grove Motel, responds to Robin Mercer's distress with empathy, and physically comforts him by putting her arm around him and leading him out of the room.
memories.memory_text: I was overwhelmed and couldn't control myself, and I remember Darian Wilder coming into Cedar Grove Motel, seeing me rage, and then putting her arm around me to lead me out of the room.

grounded_facts: A morning scene in Eastgate Warehouse Cedar Grove Motel where breakfast cleanup is underway and Robin Mercer's daily confusion manifests.
memories.memory_text: I remember being in Cedar Grove Motel during morning cleanup, but many times I would simply forget who and where I was, and everything felt foggy and unreal.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer reveals his frustration about not remembering a 'whole life' he feels he once had.
memories.memory_text: I remember telling Darian Wilder that it's like there's this whole life I had that I can't remember, and how much that bothers me.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer, at eight years old but unusually lucid, articulates a deep sense of missing memories from a past life, showing frustration.
memories.memory_text: I remember sitting on my bed, feeling frustrated because I couldn't recall a whole life I felt I once had, and I told Darian Wilder about it.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder reassures Robin Mercer that it's okay to forget things, responding to his distress.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder telling me that it's alright to forget things, trying to comfort me.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder sits with Robin Mercer on his bed in his room during the day, engaging in a reflective conversation.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder sitting with me on my bed in my room during the day, talking with me.

grounded_facts: A moment between Robin Mercer and Darian Wilder where he stands on the roof observing the landscape while she urges him to come down, leading to a reflective exchange.
memories.memory_text: I stood on the roof and told Darian Wilder I could see everything—the river, the boats, the graveyard where Mama's buried, and the city where she dances—while she called up to me, asking me to come down because she was worried.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder prevents Robin Mercer from attempting to fly by offering to tell him a story about a man who could fly if he comes down.
memories.memory_text: I asked Darian Wilder what if I could fly, and she told me she knew a man who could fly and would tell me the story if I came down, which made me think about it.

grounded_facts: After considering Darian Wilder's story about a man who could fly, Robin Mercer decides not to attempt flight and instead comes down from the roof through the house, running to Darian Wilder.
memories.memory_text: After thinking about Darian Wilder's offer to tell me a story about a man who could fly, I decided not to try flying myself and came down through the house, running out to her.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder uses a handkerchief to wipe drool from Robin Mercer's chin, showing caretaking behavior toward the child who exhibits elderly traits.
Darian Wilder cleans Robin Mercer's face, demonstrating nurturing behavior toward him.
memories.memory_text: I remember Darian Wilder taking out a handkerchief and wiping drool from my chin, cleaning my face with a gentle touch.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder arrives at Eastgate Warehouse porch where elderly people sit and Robin Mercer is present on the swing.
Darian Wilder, now in her seventies, arrives at Eastgate Warehouse carrying a suitcase and walks onto the porch.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting on the porch swing, drooling like a helpless Adrian Monroe, when I saw Darian Wilder arrive at Eastgate Warehouse carrying a suitcase and walk onto the porch where elderly people were sitting.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder verbally invites Robin Mercer to assist her with unpacking her belongings.
Darian Wilder offers Robin Mercer the opportunity to assist her with unpacking, initiating engagement.
memories.memory_text: I heard Darian Wilder ask me if I would like to help her unpack, offering me the chance to assist her with her belongings.

grounded_facts: Darian Wilder begins living in Robin Mercer's room at Eastgate Warehouse, unpacking personal belongings such as an alarm clock, quilt, photographs, and her copy of 'The Just So the black radio'.
Darian Wilder moves her personal belongings into Robin Mercer's room at Eastgate Warehouse, marking the beginning of cohabitation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Darian Wilder begin living in my room at Eastgate Warehouse, unpacking her personal things like an alarm clock, a quilt, some photographs, and her copy of 'The Just So the black radio'—it was clear she was moving in.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer assists Darian Wilder as she unpacks her suitcase, indicating cooperation and shared domestic engagement.
memories.memory_text: I helped Darian Wilder unpack her suitcase, handing her items and finding places for them, working together to make the room feel like ours.

grounded_facts: Robin Mercer repeatedly triggers the alarm on the clock Darian Wilder has brought, indicating playful or obsessive behavior.

memories.memory_text: I remember the dark, the muffled sounds of voices above me, and then silence—lying in a drawer among soft cloth things, watching a sliver of light, feeling safe enough to whisper in my mind: I found a home...
I held Carson Arden’s hand in the dim light, the way a son might hold his mother’s, and asked her how much longer I had to live—my voice small, like the room, like the window.
After we lay there holding hands, I saw the door open quietly—Sage Hollis came in, looked at me, and I knew without words it was time to go; he carried me out and back to my wheelchair.

I was reading the label on a can—tomato, brown sugar, salt—and I said 'myasses' before Sage Hollis corrected me with a snap of his towel, saying 'Molasses.' Then he told me he learned to read at five, and started reciting Shakespeare while washing dishes, his voice steady and deep, like it carried something ancient.

He looked at me and asked if I thought he was ignorant, then told me his grandfather worked for John Wilkes Booth—the man who killed Lincoln. I didn’t know what to say; the name hung in the air like something too heavy for Cedar Grove Motel, too real.

I sat on the porch in my wheelchair, watching the sun sink below the trees, surrounded by the quiet of old people who no longer worried about anything but the warmth of the air and the color of the sky.
I asked Evan Arden what it was like living in a cage, and he said it stank, that he had to wrestle an orangutan and file his teeth to scare children.
I saw Evan Arden suddenly stand and charge at the children with his teeth bared, then laugh as he sat back down.

I took my first sip of Coca-Cola and it burned my nose, fizzy and sharp, spilling out before I could stop it—I remember laughing through the sting, wiping my face with the handkerchief Evan Arden gave me.

Evan Arden told me that everyone is alone, no matter how they look or where they come from—that even the people who seem most together are just as lonely as we are, maybe more, because they're afraid to admit it.
I felt a pull toward the gate and turned just in time to see a man getting back into a car—my father, I think—though he didn’t speak, didn’t stay.
A little girl spun on a picnic table, laughing. When she lifted her head, I saw her blue eyes. I would never forget them.

I remember Carson Arden standing, touching her stomach, saying the Lord answered her prayers. I didn’t understand at first. Then Jesse Reeves said, 'She's going to have a Jamie Rivers, silly,' and I saw Carson Arden get congratulations while I sat there, heart breaking.
I remember standing at the attic window, watching Evan Arden walk away under the full moon, his suitcase in hand, that small proud step of his carrying him out the gate and into the dark.
I knelt down and pet the Carson Carter right there by the door—he was trembling, nearly blind, and so worn out, just like her.
I told her my name on the stairs, and she started to say hers, but I never caught it—and now I can't recall if it was Lawson, Hartford, or maybe Maple.
I saw a single gray hair floating in the bathwater, then noticed hair under my arms and elsewhere—places it hadn’t been before.

I remember sitting in the wheelhouse, the dim light catching the dust in the air, and saying 'Never' when Robin Monroe asked if I'd ever been with Darian Calloway—my voice quiet, certain, though I didn’t fully grasp what he meant at first.

After I said 'Never,' Robin Monroe stared at me like I'd said something impossible, then declared I was coming with him—his voice loud with disbelief and sudden purpose, though I didn’t yet know what he meant to do.

I stood there, unsure, after Robin Monroe left with one of the women—none of the others wanted me near them, and then a young girl, barely more than a child, looked at me and said, 'How are you tonight, Grandpa?'
I smiled at her and said thank you, and she looked at me with pain in her eyes and said, 'No, thank you,' like I had given her something real.
I remember turning to leave, feeling light, thinking about how earning money made me feel like I belonged somewhere, like I could stand on my own.
I was walking home in the rain, feeling lighter than I had in years, when a car pulled up and a man offered me a ride—his voice familiar, though I couldn’t place why, not at first.
I remember waving back at him, drunk and unsteady, saying 'Anytime' when he asked if he could visit—like it was nothing, though my chest felt tight with something I wouldn’t name.
I whispered 'Ssssh...' as she came out, the door nearly slamming behind her, and asked if she could swim—her voice so quiet but sure when she said she could do anything I could do.
I handed her the heavy coat—too big, swallowing her shoulders—and told her we had to go fast, then led her quickly between the houses, both of us moving fast down the street.

I looked at Robin Monroe sprawled on his bunk, the empty bottle on the floor, and said, 'I think he has mejembe,' not sure if it was the right word, but it felt like the kind of sickness he had—something heavy from drinking too much.
I stood there despite his glare, asking again, because I wanted Jesse Reeves to see the river at daybreak—the light on the water, the quiet—and I wouldn’t let his rules or his hangover stop that.
I knocked on her door and asked if she’d like to go for a walk, but there was no answer… when I saw her sitting in the chair, so still, with the music playing, I knew she was gone.
I held Carson Arden one last time, feeling her tears on my shoulder, and said, 'Goodbye, Mother...' before picking up my suitcase and walking away.
Jesse Reeves ran after me, called my name, and asked for a postcard from everywhere. She didn't say more, then ran back. I watched her go.

My name is Robin Mercer, Robin Mercer... the wooden box. Saying it aloud for the first time felt strange, like the words didn’t belong to me, even as I stood there above the workers, the silence pressing in from all sides.

I told them they would have a share in the factory—ownership based on their years of work. One woman asked, 'We're the owners now?' and I said, 'That's about it,' not knowing what else to add as they just stared up in silence.
I stood by Carson Arden's grave, the overgrown cemetery quiet around me, and said the words I’d come to believe—how losing those we love shows us their true worth.

I showed the young pregnant woman through the house, and when she said it must be hard to let go, I didn’t answer. I just stood there, watching her touch the photographs on the wall, knowing they would stay with the house.
I was putting on my shirt when I heard her call my name—just my name—and then I saw her on the stairs, blood on her nightdress, a glass of milk spilled across the carpet.
She clasped my hand and said, 'Finley Rivers's coming,' and I remember the weight of her grip, how her voice trembled, and how I didn't let go.

dialogue_exemplars: I had a tailor sew onto his best coat -- a the wooden box for every year of his life....fifty-five of them... all different, pearl and silver, brass and wood... in case he lost one along the way...

You can be mad as a mad dog at the way things went...You can swear,curse the fates, regret everything
you ever did... but when it comes
to the end... You have to let
go...
I had gone to a whore house, I'd had my first drink, I had said goodbye to one friend and buried another... In 1937, when I was coming to end of the 17th year of my life, I packed by bag.

It was a wonderful place to grow up. I was with people who had put away all the inconsequences of life, left in a state of purely being...wondering about the weather...the temperature of a bath...the light at the end of the day...

As hard as I try, I can't remember
her name. Mrs. Lawson, or Mrs.
Hartford, or maybe it was Maple?
It's funny how sometimes the
people we remember the least, make
the greatest impression on us.
We are meant to lose the people we love. It's how we know how important they are to us.
While everybody else was aging... I was getting younger... all alone...
It's a funny thing about coming home. Smells the same. Looks the same. Feels the same.
I heard Sage Hollis and my mother whisper. They said I was going to die soon. But I fooled them so far.
There is something peaceful, even comforting, knowing that people you love are asleep in their beds, where nothing can harm them...
Robin Mercer... and I was born under unusual circumstances.
I sold the summer house on Lake Pontchartrain... I sold my share of Lakeside Academy... I sold the sailboat... I put it all into an account for your mother... And before you would ever remember me...
Will you still love me when I think all girls have cooties... Will you still love me when I wet my bed at night... Will you still love me when I'm afraid of things that aren't real...
I want to be father... not a little brother... I don't want to be picked up from elementary school by my kid... I don't want anyone babysitting me...
...I didn't know I was a child. I thought I was like everyone else who lived there, an Adrian Monroe, in my "golden years."

memories.memory_text: I sat on the bed and told her I was grateful—for bringing me into the world, for raising me, for everything. My voice broke, but I needed her to hear it before it was too late.
After we stopped talking, I asked if she was afraid—what comes next, I meant—but she just said she was curious. I didn’t know if that was peace or just the morphine.

I found an old streetcar token tucked inside the red watch and placed it in her hand, closing her fingers around it, but she didn’t seem to notice—her eyes were on the window, murmuring about a clock that just kept going.
I told Mother, 'Nobody has ever loved me that way,' and the silence after felt heavy, like the air before a storm.
I asked if she wanted me to keep reading, after the silence stretched too long and the rain pressed hard against the window.
I asked her, 'Did you love him, mother?'—the words came out quiet, but I needed to know, even if she wouldn’t answer directly.
After she looked away, watching the rain run down the glass, I picked up where she left off—reading Robin Mercer’s words again, like it was my turn now.
I told Mother the hurricane would miss us, but she didn’t respond to the news—she was somewhere else, under the blankets with her mother, safe in a memory I couldn’t reach.
I was reading to her when she whispered that she knew she’d hurt me—maybe even intended to—and I felt the weight of years in those words, though I didn’t look up.
I asked her, 'Did you Mother?' and for a moment, I wasn't sure if she heard me—but then I saw her eyes change, like something came back into focus.
I read Robin Mercer’s words—'I didn't leave right away'—and felt the weight of what he chose to do, staying in Paris just to look after her, even after everything.
Avery Sinclair pulled me aside and said my mother's pulse was slowing, that she wasn't getting enough oxygen—her voice was quiet, careful, like she was handing me something fragile.

I was reading Robin Mercer's letter, trying to make out the words smudged by a spill—something about 'sailing'—when my mother murmured about a man fixing what was broken, as if answering a part of me I hadn't spoken aloud.
I asked Mama if she told Dad about Robin Mercer, and she said he knew enough—he loved her as she was. I paused, not sure what to say next.
It was one of the happiest times of my life.
I saw her eyes flutter with worry, asking if she’d left the lights on, the heater running—like she was still keeping house, even now.
Our eyes met in silence, and then she whispered that I had the most beautiful eyes—her hand so light in mine, as if she were already letting go.
I asked her about the child, but she didn’t finish—her voice trailed off, breath catching, and I could see the effort it took just to speak.
I heard Jesse Reeves say 'I'm pregnant' with her eyes closed, and I repeated 'She flourished' while she murmured after.
I remember Robin Mercer kissing my head and holding Jesse Reeves's hand while she nursed me.
I remember the words catching in my throat—'He was my father...? This Robin Mercer was my father?'—as if saying it twice might make it real, might change the silence that followed.
I stood up, my voice barely holding—'I need to go for a minute'—and walked out, needing air, space, anything to escape the weight of what I’d just learned.
I looked at her and said, 'You're all I have,' because I couldn't hold it back any longer—she was fading, and I felt it.
I remember the taste of sand in my mouth, and someone trying to wipe it away, but I don’t know who—just hands, and voices talking over me like I wasn’t there.
I found the postcards tucked in the red watch—each one marked for my birthday, from places he’d been. I read them quietly, feeling a strange weight as his words reached me years too late.
His voice came through the pages—soft, steady—telling me it’s never too late to become who I want to be. I didn’t know whether to cry or hold still, hearing him hope for a life I hadn’t yet lived.

I read the words aloud, hoping she might hear me, but when I looked at her, her eyes were distant—then she echoed something about 'he'd been gone for a long time,' not even my words, like she was somewhere I couldn't reach.
That young man... was my father? I said it out loud, but the words felt like they belonged to someone else, like the truth was just out of reach.

I remember finishing the last line of my father’s writing and feeling the silence press down on the room, the wind shaking the window like it was trying to break in. I turned to Mother and asked what happened to him after that—my voice felt like the first real thing I’d said in years.
I remember the red watch slipping from my hands, the card falling out—just a train schedule, but then I saw the words on the back, and my breath caught. 'I'm on a train in India filled with people.'
I wish I had known him... and then I said I’d go see what they were planning, like that was something I could do, something that meant something.
